entry.sum: Three basic questions about a network are answered by short greedy or layer-by-layer procedures: breadth-first and depth-first search decide reachability, Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths when edge weights are non-negative, and Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms find a minimum spanning tree. The idea to remember is that each algorithm is correct because of one invariant: settled distances never change, and every edge chosen is the cheapest edge across some cut.
key: d(s,v) = \min_{u:\,uv \in E}\bigl(d(s,u) + w(uv)\bigr)\quad (v \ne s,\ \text{no negative cycles})
e \text{ cheapest edge across a cut } (S, V\setminus S) \;\Rightarrow\; e \text{ lies in some minimum spanning tree}
entry.why: Route planners, network routing protocols, circuit and pipeline design and project scheduling all reduce to shortest paths, spanning trees or longest paths in acyclic graphs, and these algorithms are the standard first examples of proving an algorithm correct.

links.note: Shortest paths and minimum spanning trees are linear programs whose optimal solutions can be taken integral, and the greedy proof for spanning trees is the prototype of greedy optimisation over a matroid.
Kirchhoff's matrix-tree theorem counts the spanning trees of a graph as any cofactor of its Laplacian matrix.

refs: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest & Stein, Introduction to Algorithms
Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications

blocks.body:
A map of towns joined by roads of known lengths is a weighted graph. Three questions come up again and again. Can I get from town $s$ to town $t$ at all? What is the shortest route? And if I want to lay cable so that every town is connected, using as little cable as possible, which roads should the cable follow?

Each has a fast algorithm that can also be run by hand on a small example; this page explains them and, above all, why they are correct. We use the vocabulary of [[graph-basics]] and the idea of running time from [[algorithms]].

blocks.title: Searching a graph: BFS and DFS
blocks.body:
Start at a vertex $s$. Breadth-first search (BFS) visits $s$, then all neighbours of $s$, then all their unvisited neighbours, and so on, in layers. It keeps a queue: take the vertex at the front, put each of its unvisited neighbours at the back and mark them visited. Depth-first search (DFS) instead keeps going forward from the most recently found vertex, and backtracks only when it gets stuck; it uses a stack (or recursion) instead of a queue.

Both visit exactly the vertices reachable from $s$, and both look at each edge a bounded number of times, so they run in time $O(|V| + |E|)$ when the graph is stored as adjacency lists. BFS gives more: the layer in which a vertex is first reached is its distance from $s$ counted in edges. The reason is that layer $k+1$ consists of the unvisited neighbours of layer $k$, so by induction every vertex in layer $k$ has a path of $k$ edges from $s$ and none shorter.

The edges along which vertices are discovered form a BFS or DFS tree, so search also finds a spanning tree of a connected graph in linear time.

blocks.title: Weighted graph and distance
blocks.body:
A weighted graph is a graph (directed or undirected) together with a weight $w(e)$ for each edge $e$. The length of a path is the sum of the weights of its edges. The distance $d(s,v)$ is the minimum length of a path from $s$ to $v$ (and $+\infty$ if there is none).

If all weights equal 1, BFS computes distances. With general weights a path with more edges can be shorter.

blocks.title: Dijkstra's algorithm
blocks.body:
Suppose all weights are non-negative. Dijkstra's algorithm grows a set of settled vertices whose distances are known. Every vertex $v$ carries a label $L(v)$, the length of the best path to $v$ found so far: initially $L(s) = 0$ and $L(v) = \infty$ for $v \ne s$.

1. Among the unsettled vertices, choose one, $u$, with the smallest label, and settle it.
2. For every edge $uv$ with $v$ unsettled, replace $L(v)$ by $\min\bigl(L(v),\, L(u) + w(uv)\bigr)$. This is called relaxing the edge.
3. Repeat until every vertex is settled (or the smallest label is $\infty$).

Recording, for each $v$, the vertex $u$ that last lowered $L(v)$ lets you read off the shortest paths themselves: they form a shortest-path tree rooted at $s$.

Here is the graph we will use throughout. Its vertices are $A, \dots, F$ and its edges, with weights, are
$$AB\,4,\ AC\,2,\ BC\,1,\ BD\,5,\ CD\,8,\ CE\,10,\ DE\,2,\ DF\,6,\ EF\,3.$$
Running Dijkstra from $A$, the labels change as follows (a dash means settled).

1. Settle $A$ (0). Labels: $B = 4$, $C = 2$.
2. Settle $C$ (2). $B$ improves to $2 + 1 = 3$; $D = 10$, $E = 12$.
3. Settle $B$ (3). $D$ improves to $3 + 5 = 8$.
4. Settle $D$ (8). $E$ improves to $8 + 2 = 10$; $F = 14$.
5. Settle $E$ (10). $F$ improves to $10 + 3 = 13$.
6. Settle $F$ (13).

So $d(A,F) = 13$ along $A, C, B, D, E, F$. Notice that the direct edge $AB$ of weight 4 is beaten by the two-edge route through $C$.

blocks.title: Correctness of Dijkstra's algorithm
blocks.body: If every edge weight is non-negative, then at the moment a vertex $u$ is settled, $L(u) = d(s,u)$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
First, every finite label is the length of an actual walk from $s$ (labels are only ever set to $L(u) + w(uv)$ for an already-labelled $u$), so always $L(v) \ge d(s,v)$.

We prove the theorem by induction on the order of settling. The vertex $s$ is settled first with $L(s) = 0 = d(s,s)$. Now let $u \neq s$ be the next vertex settled, and assume all previously settled vertices have correct labels. If $d(s,u) = \infty$ there is nothing to prove, so take a shortest path $P$ from $s$ to $u$. It starts in the settled set and ends outside it, so it has a first vertex $y$ that is not settled; let $x$ be the vertex just before $y$ on $P$. Then $x$ is settled, so $L(x) = d(s,x)$, and when $x$ was settled the edge $xy$ was relaxed, giving
$$L(y) \le d(s,x) + w(xy) = d(s,y),$$
where the equality holds because the part of $P$ from $s$ to $y$ is itself a shortest path. Since weights are non-negative, the rest of $P$ from $y$ to $u$ has length at least 0, so $d(s,y) \le d(s,u)$. Finally $u$ was chosen with the smallest label among unsettled vertices, so $L(u) \le L(y)$. Putting these together,
$$L(u) \le L(y) \le d(s,y) \le d(s,u) \le L(u),$$
so all are equal and $L(u) = d(s,u)$.

blocks.title: Spanning tree and minimum spanning tree
blocks.body:
A spanning tree of a connected graph $G = (V,E)$ is a subgraph that is a tree and contains every vertex; it has exactly $|V| - 1$ edges. If the edges have weights, a minimum spanning tree (MST) is a spanning tree whose total weight is as small as possible.

A cut is a partition of $V$ into a non-empty set $S$ and its non-empty complement $V \setminus S$; an edge crosses the cut if it has one end in each part.

blocks.title: Cut lemma
blocks.body: Let $F$ be a set of edges contained in some minimum spanning tree of a connected weighted graph. Let $S$ be a cut that no edge of $F$ crosses, and let $e$ be an edge of minimum weight among those crossing $S$. Then $F \cup \{e\}$ is also contained in some minimum spanning tree.

blocks.title: Proof of the cut lemma
blocks.body: Let $T$ be a minimum spanning tree containing $F$. If $e \in T$ we are done. Otherwise adding $e = uv$ to $T$ creates exactly one cycle, made of $e$ and the path in $T$ from $u$ to $v$. That path starts in $S$ and ends outside it (because $e$ crosses the cut), so it uses some edge $f$ that also crosses the cut. By the choice of $e$, $w(e) \le w(f)$. Removing $f$ breaks the cycle, so $T' = T + e - f$ is again a spanning tree, of weight $w(T) + w(e) - w(f) \le w(T)$. Hence $T'$ is also a minimum spanning tree. It contains $F$, because $f$ crosses the cut and no edge of $F$ does, and it contains $e$.

blocks.title: Kruskal and Prim
blocks.body:
Both algorithms add edges one at a time, and the cut lemma shows that after each step the chosen edges still lie in some MST; after $|V| - 1$ steps they form one.

Kruskal's algorithm: sort the edges by weight and go through them in that order, adding an edge whenever it does not form a cycle with the edges already chosen. When Kruskal adds $e = uv$, let $S$ be the set of vertices joined to $u$ by chosen edges. No chosen edge crosses $S$, and any cheaper edge crossing $S$ would have joined two different pieces when it was examined and so would have been added. So $e$ is a cheapest edge across $S$, and the cut lemma applies. With a union-find structure to detect cycles, the running time is $O(|E| \log |E|)$, dominated by sorting.

Prim's algorithm: grow a single tree from a starting vertex, each time adding the cheapest edge with exactly one end in the current tree. Here the cut is simply the current tree's vertex set. Implemented with a heap it runs in $O(|E| \log |V|)$, and it is the algorithm of choice when the graph is given as a distance table.

On our graph Kruskal examines $BC\,1$ (add), $AC\,2$ (add), $DE\,2$ (add), $EF\,3$ (add), $AB\,4$ (reject: cycle $A,B,C$), $BD\,5$ (add). Five edges have been chosen, so we stop: the MST is $\{BC, AC, DE, EF, BD\}$ with weight 13. Prim from $A$ picks $AC$, $CB$, $BD$, $DE$, $EF$ in that order and finds the same tree.

blocks.title: Acyclic graphs, critical paths and negative weights
blocks.body:
In a directed graph with no directed cycles, the vertices can be listed in a topological order in which every edge points forward (repeatedly remove a vertex with no incoming edges; this takes linear time). Then shortest and longest paths are easy: set $L(s) = 0$, process the vertices in that order, and for each later vertex $v$ set its label to the best of $L(u) + w(uv)$ over incoming edges $uv$. Every incoming neighbour has already been finished, so one pass suffices, even with negative weights.

Critical path analysis uses this for projects. Each activity has a duration and a list of activities that must finish before it starts. The earliest start of an activity is the longest path to it in the precedence network; the project's minimum duration is the longest path overall, and the activities on such a path are critical: delaying any of them delays the whole project. An activity's float is how much it can slip without delaying the project.

In a general graph with negative weights Dijkstra can fail (see the pitfalls), but the Bellman–Ford algorithm still works: relax every edge, $|V| - 1$ times over. This takes $O(|V||E|)$ time, and one more round that still lowers some label reveals a negative cycle reachable from $s$, in which case shortest paths to the vertices reachable from that cycle do not exist.

blocks.title: A small project
blocks.body: A project has five activities: $P$ (3 days), $Q$ (2 days), $R$ (4 days, after $P$), $S$ (2 days, after $P$ and $Q$) and $U$ (3 days, after $R$ and $S$). Find the minimum project duration, the critical activities, and the float of $Q$ and of $S$.
blocks.solution:
Earliest starts, in topological order: $P$ and $Q$ start at 0. $R$ starts when $P$ ends, at 3. $S$ needs both $P$ (ends 3) and $Q$ (ends 2), so it starts at $\max(3,2) = 3$. $U$ needs $R$ (ends 7) and $S$ (ends 5), so it starts at 7 and ends at 10. The minimum duration is 10 days.

Latest starts, working backwards from 10: $U$ must start by 7. $R$ must end by 7, so start by 3; $S$ must end by 7, so start by 5. $P$ must end by $\min(3, 5) = 3$, so start by 0; $Q$ must end by 5, so start by 3.

An activity is critical when its earliest and latest starts agree: $P$, $R$, $U$, the path of length $3 + 4 + 3 = 10$. The float of $Q$ is $3 - 0 = 3$ days and the float of $S$ is $5 - 3 = 2$ days.

blocks.title: Distinct weights force a unique MST
blocks.body: Prove that if all edge weights of a connected graph are different, the graph has exactly one minimum spanning tree.
blocks.solution:
Suppose $T \ne T'$ are both minimum spanning trees. They have the same number of edges, so each has an edge the other lacks. Among all edges in exactly one of $T$, $T'$, let $e$ be the lightest; by symmetry say $e \in T \setminus T'$.

Adding $e$ to $T'$ creates a cycle. Not every edge of this cycle lies in $T$, since $T$ has no cycles, so the cycle contains an edge $f \in T' \setminus T$. Then $f$ is also in exactly one of the trees, so $w(f) > w(e)$ by the choice of $e$ and distinctness. Now $T' + e - f$ is a spanning tree (removing an edge of the only cycle keeps it connected) of weight $w(T') + w(e) - w(f) < w(T')$, contradicting the minimality of $T'$. Hence $T = T'$.

The same exchange shows a useful fact: with distinct weights, the heaviest edge of any cycle belongs to no MST.

blocks.body:
- Dijkstra needs non-negative weights. With directed edges $s \to a$ of weight 2, $s \to b$ of weight 3 and $b \to a$ of weight $-2$, Dijkstra settles $a$ with label 2, but $d(s,a) = 1$ via $b$. Adding a constant to every weight does not fix this: it penalises paths with more edges.
- A shortest-path tree is not a minimum spanning tree. In a triangle with $AB = AC = 3$ and $BC = 1$, the shortest-path tree from $A$ uses $AB$ and $AC$ (weight 6), while an MST uses $BC$ and one other edge (weight 4).
- Greedy does not always work. Choosing the nearest unvisited town at each step (nearest neighbour) can give a poor travelling-salesman tour; no polynomial-time algorithm is known for that problem.

Shortest paths and spanning trees are linear programs in disguise; see [[linear-programming]]. Replacing edge lengths by capacities leads to [[network-flows]] and the max-flow min-cut theorem, whose augmenting-path algorithms use BFS as a subroutine. Search and spanning trees appear throughout [[cycles-matchings]] and [[planar-graphs]], and the contrast between these efficient algorithms and the travelling-salesman problem is a concrete entry point to [[p-vs-np]].

1. Run BFS from $A$ on the graph of this page, ignoring weights, and list the layers. Then run Dijkstra from $D$ and find the shortest route from $D$ to $A$.
2. Find all minimum spanning trees of the complete graph on vertices $1,2,3,4$ where edge $ij$ has weight $i + j$.
3. Show that in a connected graph with distinct weights, the cheapest edge at each vertex belongs to the MST.
4. Explain why Bellman–Ford needs at most $|V| - 1$ rounds when there is no negative cycle.

entry.sum: A flow sends material from a source $s$ to a sink $t$ through a directed network without exceeding any edge's capacity and without loss at intermediate vertices. The max-flow min-cut theorem says the largest possible flow value equals the smallest total capacity of a set of edges whose removal separates $s$ from $t$, and a flow is maximum exactly when no augmenting path remains.
key: |f| = f(S \to T) - f(T \to S) \le c(S,T) \quad\text{for every flow } f \text{ and cut } (S,T)
entry.why: Maximum flow models transport, communication and scheduling capacity, and through the integrality theorem it proves combinatorial min-max theorems such as Menger's theorem, Hall's marriage theorem and König's theorem on bipartite matchings.

links.note: The vertex-edge incidence matrix of a directed graph is totally unimodular, which is the linear-algebra reason that flow linear programs with integer capacities have integer optimal vertices.

In statistical physics the ground state of a ferromagnetic Ising model in a random external field is a minimum $s$–$t$ cut of an associated network, so it can be computed exactly with maximum-flow algorithms.

refs: Ahuja, Magnanti & Orlin, Network Flows: Theory, Algorithms, and Applications

blocks.body:
Water flows from a reservoir $s$ to a city $t$ through a system of one-way pipes, each with a maximum rate. How much water per second can reach the city? An obvious upper bound comes from any set of pipes that, if blocked, would cut the city off: the flow can be no larger than their total capacity. The surprise is that the best such bound is always achieved.

This is the max-flow min-cut theorem. Its proof is also an algorithm, and its integer version turns many problems about matchings and disjoint paths into flow problems. We use directed graphs and graph search from [[graph-algorithms]].

blocks.title: Network and flow
blocks.body:
A network is a directed graph with two special vertices, a source $s$ and a sink $t$, and a capacity $c(u,v) \ge 0$ on each edge $(u,v)$. A flow is an assignment of numbers $f(u,v)$ to the edges such that

1. (capacity) $0 \le f(u,v) \le c(u,v)$ for every edge;
2. (conservation) at every vertex $v \ne s, t$, the total flow in equals the total flow out.

The value $|f|$ is the net flow out of $s$: the flow on edges leaving $s$ minus the flow on edges entering $s$.

blocks.title: Cut
blocks.body:
An $s$–$t$ cut is a partition of the vertices into sets $S$ and $T$ with $s \in S$ and $t \in T$. Its capacity $c(S,T)$ is the sum of the capacities of edges going from $S$ to $T$. Edges from $T$ back to $S$ do not count.

For a flow $f$ write $f(S \to T)$ for the total flow on edges from $S$ to $T$, and $f(T \to S)$ for the reverse direction.

blocks.title: Flow across a cut
blocks.body:
For every flow $f$ and every $s$–$t$ cut $(S,T)$,
$$|f| = f(S \to T) - f(T \to S) \le c(S,T).$$

Add up, over all vertices $v \in S$, the quantity (flow out of $v$) minus (flow into $v$). For $v = s$ this is $|f|$, and for every other $v \in S$ it is 0 by conservation, so the sum is $|f|$. On the other hand, an edge with both ends in $S$ contributes $+f$ at its tail and $-f$ at its head, so cancels. An edge from $S$ to $T$ contributes $+f$ once, and an edge from $T$ to $S$ contributes $-f$ once. Hence the sum equals $f(S \to T) - f(T \to S)$. Finally $f(S \to T) \le c(S,T)$ by the capacity condition and $f(T \to S) \ge 0$.

blocks.title: Why greedy is not enough: residual networks
blocks.body:
A natural idea is to keep finding paths from $s$ to $t$ with spare capacity and pushing flow along them. Consider edges $s \to a$, $s \to b$, $a \to b$, $a \to t$, $b \to t$, all of capacity 1. If we first push 1 unit along $s, a, b, t$, then every $s$–$t$ path in the graph uses a full edge and we are stuck at value 1. But value 2 is possible, along $s, a, t$ and $s, b, t$.

The fix is to allow flow to be sent back, cancelling an earlier choice. Given a flow $f$, the residual network has, for each edge $(u,v)$,

- a forward edge $u \to v$ with residual capacity $c(u,v) - f(u,v)$ if this is positive, and
- a backward edge $v \to u$ with residual capacity $f(u,v)$ if this is positive.

An augmenting path is an $s$–$t$ path in the residual network. Pushing $\delta$ units along it (where $\delta$ is the smallest residual capacity on the path) means increasing $f$ on forward edges and decreasing it on backward edges by $\delta$. Capacities stay respected, conservation still holds at each inner vertex, and the value rises by $\delta$. In the example, after the first path the residual network contains $s \to b \to a \to t$, using the backward edge $b \to a$; pushing 1 unit along it removes the flow on $a \to b$ and gives value 2.

(If the network has both $u \to v$ and $v \to u$, keep their residual edges separate; nothing changes in the argument.)

blocks.title: Max-flow min-cut theorem (Ford–Fulkerson)

blocks.body:
(1 implies 2) An augmenting path would increase the value, so a maximum flow has none.

(2 implies 3) Let $S$ be the set of vertices reachable from $s$ in the residual network and $T$ the rest. Then $t \in T$ since there is no augmenting path. Take an edge $(u,v)$ with $u \in S$, $v \in T$. If $f(u,v) < c(u,v)$ there would be a residual edge $u \to v$ and $v$ would be reachable; so $f(u,v) = c(u,v)$. Take an edge $(v,u)$ with $v \in T$, $u \in S$. If $f(v,u) > 0$ there would be a backward residual edge $u \to v$; so $f(v,u) = 0$. By the previous theorem, $|f| = f(S \to T) - f(T \to S) = c(S,T) - 0$.

(3 implies 1) Every flow $g$ satisfies $|g| \le c(S,T) = |f|$ by the previous theorem.

For a finite network a maximum flow exists: the set of flows is a closed bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}^E$ and the value is a continuous function, so it attains its maximum. Applying (1 implies 3) to it gives a cut of the same capacity, and no cut can have smaller capacity than a flow's value.

blocks.title: Integrality theorem
blocks.body: If all capacities are integers, the Ford–Fulkerson method (start from the zero flow and augment while an augmenting path exists) stops after at most $c(\{s\}, V \setminus \{s\})$ augmentations, and the final flow is a maximum flow with every $f(u,v)$ an integer.

By induction all flow values stay integers: residual capacities are then integers, so the bottleneck $\delta$ is a positive integer. Each augmentation therefore raises $|f|$ by at least 1, and $|f|$ can never exceed the capacity of the cut $(\{s\}, V \setminus \{s\})$, so the method stops. When it stops there is no augmenting path, and by the max-flow min-cut theorem the flow is maximum.

blocks.title: Algorithms and modelling tricks
A maximum flow and its certificate
blocks.body: The network has edges $s \to a$ (10), $s \to b$ (8), $a \to b$ (5), $a \to c$ (6), $b \to d$ (9), $c \to t$ (9), $d \to c$ (4), $d \to t$ (7). Find a maximum flow and a cut proving it is maximum.
blocks.solution:
Augment along paths with spare capacity:

1. $s, a, c, t$: bottleneck $a \to c$, push 6.
2. $s, a, b, d, t$: $s \to a$ has 4 left, push 4.
3. $s, b, d, t$: $d \to t$ has 3 left, push 3.
4. $s, b, d, c, t$: $b \to d$ has 2 left, push 2.

Total value $6 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 15$. On the edges: $s \to a$ 10, $s \to b$ 5, $a \to b$ 4, $a \to c$ 6, $b \to d$ 9, $c \to t$ 8, $d \to c$ 2, $d \to t$ 7; at each of $a, b, c, d$ inflow equals outflow.

In the residual network, from $s$ we can reach $b$ (since $s \to b$ has 3 spare) and then $a$ (backward along $a \to b$, which carries 4), but nothing else: $a \to c$ and $b \to d$ are full. So $S = \{s, a, b\}$, and the edges leaving $S$ are $a \to c$ (6) and $b \to d$ (9), total 15. A cut of capacity 15 matches the flow of value 15, so both are optimal.

blocks.title: König's theorem from max-flow min-cut
blocks.body: In a bipartite graph with parts $L$ and $R$, a vertex cover is a set of vertices touching every edge. Prove that the largest matching has the same size as the smallest vertex cover.
blocks.solution:
A matching of size $m$ needs at least $m$ vertices to cover its own edges, which are disjoint, so max matching $\le$ min cover. For the reverse inequality, build a network: edges $s \to u$ of capacity 1 for $u \in L$, edges $v \to t$ of capacity 1 for $v \in R$, and each graph edge $uv$ directed $u \to v$ with a huge capacity, say $|L| + 1$.

By the integrality theorem there is an integer maximum flow; each $u \in L$ receives at most 1 unit, so it uses at most one edge out of $u$, and similarly at $v \in R$. The edges $u \to v$ carrying flow form a matching whose size is the flow value.

Now take a minimum cut $(S,T)$. The cut $(\{s\}, \text{rest})$ has capacity $|L|$, so the minimum cut has capacity at most $|L|$ and cannot contain a huge edge. So if $u \in L \cap S$ and $uv$ is an edge, then $v \in S$. The edges leaving $S$ are therefore $s \to u$ for $u \in L \cap T$ and $v \to t$ for $v \in R \cap S$, and the capacity is $|L \cap T| + |R \cap S|$. The set $(L \cap T) \cup (R \cap S)$ is a vertex cover: an edge $uv$ with $u \notin T$ has $u \in S$, hence $v \in R \cap S$. Hence
$$\text{min cover} \le c(S,T) = \text{max flow} \le \text{max matching}.$$

blocks.title: Regular bipartite graphs have perfect matchings
blocks.body: Let $G$ be a bipartite graph with parts $L$, $R$ in which every vertex has degree $k \ge 1$. Prove that $G$ has a perfect matching.
blocks.solution:
Counting edges from each side gives $k|L| = k|R|$, so $|L| = |R|$. Use the network of the previous example. Put flow $1$ on each edge $s \to u$ and $v \to t$, and flow $1/k$ on each graph edge. Every $u \in L$ receives 1 and sends out $k \cdot \frac1k = 1$; every $v \in R$ receives $k \cdot \frac1k = 1$ and sends 1. This is a flow of value $|L|$.

So the maximum flow value is at least $|L|$, and it is at most $|L|$ by the cut $(\{s\}, \text{rest})$. By the integrality theorem there is an integer flow of value $|L|$, which is a matching covering all of $L$, and hence (as $|L| = |R|$) a perfect matching. The fractional flow was only a witness; integrality did the real work.

blocks.body:
- Cut capacity counts only edges from $S$ to $T$. Edges pointing back from $T$ into $S$ add nothing.
- Without backward residual edges, repeatedly pushing along paths can get stuck below the maximum, as in the five-edge example above.
- A minimum cut need not be unique, and neither need a maximum flow; the theorem only says their values agree.
- The integrality theorem says some maximum flow is integral, not every one: with edges $s \to a$, $s \to b$, $a \to c$, $b \to c$, $c \to t$ all of capacity 1, sending $\frac12$ along each of the routes through $a$ and through $b$ is also a maximum flow.

Max-flow min-cut is linear programming duality for one particular pair of programs; see [[linear-programming]] and [[convex-optimisation]]. Through the integrality theorem it proves Hall's theorem and König's theorem from [[cycles-matchings]], and Menger's theorem on disjoint paths. Minimum-cost flows, which add a price per unit on each edge, combine these ideas with the shortest-path algorithms of [[graph-algorithms]], and the running-time questions belong to [[algorithms]].

entry.sum: Ellipses, parabolas and hyperbolas are the curves cut from a double cone by a plane, the curves whose distance to a focus is a fixed multiple $e$ of their distance to a directrix, and (apart from degenerate cases) the curves given by equations of degree two in $x$ and $y$. The eccentricity $e$ decides the type: $e<1$ ellipse, $e=1$ parabola, $e>1$ hyperbola, with the circle as the limiting case $e=0$.
entry.why: Planets and comets move on conics with the Sun at a focus, satellite dishes and headlamps use the reflective property of the parabola, and the classification of degree-two curves is the first example of simplifying a quadratic form by rotating axes.

links.note: Under an inverse-square force a body moves on a conic with the centre of force at a focus, so orbits are ellipses, parabolas or hyperbolas according to their energy (Kepler's first law for bound orbits).

Writing the quadratic part as $\mathbf{x}^{T} M \mathbf{x}$ with a symmetric matrix $M$ and diagonalising $M$ by a rotation puts any conic in standard form; the signs of the eigenvalues give the type.

blocks.body:
Shine a torch at a wall. Held straight on, the lit patch is a circle; tilt the torch and it stretches into an ellipse; tilt further and one end runs off to infinity in a parabola, then the edge opens into a hyperbola. The beam is a cone of light, the wall is a plane, and these are the conic sections.

The Greeks studied them as slices of a cone. About eighteen centuries after Apollonius wrote his books on conics, Kepler found that planets move on ellipses, and the coordinate geometry of Descartes and Fermat showed that conics are, apart from degenerate cases, exactly the curves of degree two. This page connects the three descriptions: slices, focus and directrix, and equations. It uses coordinates from [[analytic-geometry]] and completing the square from [[quadratics]].

blocks.title: Distances to foci
blocks.body:
Tie a loop of string around two pins and pull it tight with a pencil: as you move the pencil, the sum of its distances to the two pins stays fixed, and the pencil draws an ellipse. The pins are its foci. If instead the difference of the distances stays fixed, you get a hyperbola. A parabola has one focus and a line, the directrix, and consists of the points equally far from both.

Place the foci at $(\pm c, 0)$ and call the fixed sum or difference $2a$. A point $(x,y)$ on the $x$-axis with distance sum $2a$ is at $(\pm a, 0)$, so $a$ is the distance from the centre to the ends of the long axis. For the ellipse we need $a > c$; for the hyperbola $a < c$.

blocks.title: Standard equations
blocks.body:
1. The points whose distances to $(\pm c, 0)$ add up to $2a$, where $a > c \ge 0$, form the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ with $b^2 = a^2 - c^2$.
2. The points whose distances to $(\pm c, 0)$ differ by $2a$ (in either order), where $0 < a < c$, form the hyperbola $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ with $b^2 = c^2 - a^2$. Its asymptotes are $y = \pm \frac{b}{a} x$.
3. The points equally distant from $(a, 0)$ and the line $x = -a$, where $a > 0$, form the parabola $y^2 = 4ax$.

blocks.title: Proof for the ellipse
blocks.body:
Write $d_1 = \sqrt{(x+c)^2 + y^2}$ and $d_2 = \sqrt{(x-c)^2 + y^2}$. Note $d_1^2 - d_2^2 = 4cx$.

Suppose $d_1 + d_2 = 2a$. Dividing $d_1^2 - d_2^2 = 4cx$ by $d_1 + d_2$ gives $d_1 - d_2 = \frac{2cx}{a}$, and adding to $d_1 + d_2 = 2a$ gives $d_1 = a + \frac{c}{a}x$. Squaring,
$$x^2 + 2cx + c^2 + y^2 = a^2 + 2cx + \frac{c^2}{a^2}x^2,$$
so $x^2\left(1 - \frac{c^2}{a^2}\right) + y^2 = a^2 - c^2$, which is $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ after dividing by $b^2 = a^2 - c^2$.

Conversely, suppose $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$. Substituting $y^2 = b^2 - \frac{b^2}{a^2}x^2$ and $b^2 = a^2 - c^2$,
$$d_2^2 = x^2 - 2cx + c^2 + b^2 - \frac{b^2 x^2}{a^2} = \frac{c^2}{a^2}x^2 - 2cx + a^2 = \left(a - \frac{c}{a}x\right)^2.$$
Since $|x| \le a$ and $c < a$, the quantity $a - \frac{c}{a}x$ is positive, so $d_2 = a - \frac{c}{a}x$. In the same way $d_1 = a + \frac{c}{a}x$, and $d_1 + d_2 = 2a$. The hyperbola is handled the same way, and the parabola is a one-line calculation: $(x-a)^2 + y^2 = (x+a)^2$ simplifies to $y^2 = 4ax$.

blocks.title: One rule for all three: eccentricity
blocks.body:
The proof contains a hidden gem: on the ellipse, the distance to the focus $(c,0)$ is $a - \frac{c}{a}x$. Put $e = \frac{c}{a}$, the eccentricity. Then
$$PF = a - ex = e\left(\frac{a}{e} - x\right),$$
and $\frac{a}{e} - x$ is the distance from $P$ to the vertical line $x = \frac{a}{e}$. So the ellipse is the set of points whose distance to the focus is $e$ times their distance to this line, its directrix. The same computation for the hyperbola gives $e = \frac{c}{a} > 1$ with directrices $x = \pm\frac{a}{e}$, and the parabola is the case $e = 1$.

blocks.title: Focus–directrix property
blocks.body:
Given a point $F$, a line $\ell$ not through $F$ and a number $e > 0$, the set of points $P$ with $PF = e \cdot PD$, where $PD$ is the distance from $P$ to $\ell$, is an ellipse if $e < 1$, a parabola if $e = 1$ and a hyperbola if $e > 1$. With $F$ at the origin and $\ell$ the line $x = d$ ($d > 0$), its polar equation is
$$r = \frac{ed}{1 + e\cos\theta}.$$
For a hyperbola, positive $r$ gives the branch around $F$; the other branch corresponds to $1 + e\cos\theta < 0$, that is, to negative $r$.

blocks.title: Proof of the polar equation
blocks.body: A point with polar coordinates $(r, \theta)$ has $PF = r$ and $x = r\cos\theta$. Points of the curve lie on the same side of $\ell$ as $F$ (for a hyperbola, we take this branch), so $PD = d - r\cos\theta$. The condition $r = e(d - r\cos\theta)$ rearranges to $r(1 + e\cos\theta) = ed$. Converting back, $r = ed - ex$ squared gives $x^2 + y^2 = (ed - ex)^2$, that is $(1 - e^2)x^2 + 2e^2 d\,x + y^2 = e^2 d^2$. When $e = 1$ the $x^2$ term vanishes and this is a parabola. When $e \ne 1$, completing the square in $x$ gives $\frac{(x - h)^2}{\alpha} + \frac{y^2}{\beta} = 1$ with $\alpha$ and $\beta$ of the same sign if $e < 1$ (an ellipse) and of opposite signs if $e > 1$ (a hyperbola).

blocks.title: Parametric forms and tangents
The general equation of degree two
blocks.body:
Every curve $Ax^2 + Bxy + Cy^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0$ (with $A, B, C$ not all zero) is a conic or a degenerate case. The $xy$ term means the axes are tilted. Rotating the axes by an angle $\phi$ with $\cot 2\phi = \frac{A - C}{B}$ removes it, and then completing the square moves the centre to the origin. The number $B^2 - 4AC$ does not change under rotation, and it tells the type: negative for an ellipse, zero for a parabola, positive for a hyperbola. Degenerate cases also occur: $x^2 + y^2 = -1$ is empty, $x^2 - y^2 = 0$ is a pair of lines, $x^2 = 1$ is two parallel lines.

For example $xy = 1$ has $B^2 - 4AC = 1 > 0$. With $\phi = 45^\circ$, substitute $x = \frac{u - v}{\sqrt2}$, $y = \frac{u + v}{\sqrt2}$: the equation becomes $\frac{u^2 - v^2}{2} = 1$, a hyperbola with $a = b = \sqrt2$.

In the language of matrices, the quadratic part is $\mathbf{x}^T M \mathbf{x}$ with $M = \begin{pmatrix} A & B/2 \\ B/2 & C \end{pmatrix}$, the rotation diagonalises $M$, and $B^2 - 4AC = -4\det M$. So the type is decided by the signs of the eigenvalues, which is the starting point for quadric surfaces in three dimensions.

blocks.title: Back to the cone: Dandelin spheres
blocks.body:
Why do slices of a cone satisfy the two-pin rule? Here is a sketch of the argument Dandelin found in 1822. Let a plane cut one half of a circular cone in a closed curve. Two spheres fit inside the cone touching both the cone and the plane, one above the plane and one below. Each touches the cone along a horizontal circle, and touches the plane at a single point; call these points $F_1$ and $F_2$.

Take a point $P$ on the curve. The line from $P$ to the cone's apex meets the two circles at points $Q_1$ and $Q_2$. Two tangent segments drawn from the same point to a sphere have equal length, so $PF_1 = PQ_1$ and $PF_2 = PQ_2$. Hence $PF_1 + PF_2 = PQ_1 + PQ_2 = Q_1Q_2$, the distance between the two circles measured along the cone, which is the same for every $P$. So the curve is an ellipse with foci $F_1$, $F_2$: the foci are where the spheres touch the plane.

blocks.title: Reading off the features
blocks.body: Find the foci, eccentricity and directrices of $9x^2 + 25y^2 = 225$.
blocks.solution:
Divide by 225: $\frac{x^2}{25} + \frac{y^2}{9} = 1$, so $a = 5$, $b = 3$, and $c^2 = a^2 - b^2 = 16$, $c = 4$. The foci are $(\pm4, 0)$, the eccentricity is $e = \frac{c}{a} = \frac45$, and the directrices are $x = \pm\frac{a}{e} = \pm\frac{25}{4}$.

Check with the point $(0, 3)$: its distance to $(4,0)$ is 5, and its distance to $x = \frac{25}{4}$ is $\frac{25}{4}$; indeed $5 = \frac45 \cdot \frac{25}{4}$.

blocks.title: Completing the square
blocks.body: Identify the curve $x^2 + 4y^2 - 6x + 16y + 9 = 0$.
blocks.solution:
Group and complete squares: $x^2 - 6x = (x-3)^2 - 9$ and $4y^2 + 16y = 4(y+2)^2 - 16$. The equation becomes $(x-3)^2 + 4(y+2)^2 = 16$, that is
$$\frac{(x-3)^2}{16} + \frac{(y+2)^2}{4} = 1.$$
This is an ellipse with centre $(3, -2)$, $a = 4$, $b = 2$, $c = \sqrt{12} = 2\sqrt3$, so eccentricity $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and foci $(3 \pm 2\sqrt3, -2)$. As a check, $B^2 - 4AC = 0 - 16 < 0$.

blocks.title: The reflective property of the parabola
blocks.body: Let $P = (at^2, 2at)$ with $t \ne 0$ be a point on $y^2 = 4ax$ and $F = (a, 0)$ its focus. Show that the tangent at $P$ makes equal angles with $PF$ and with the horizontal line through $P$.
blocks.solution:
The tangent $ty = x + at^2$ meets the $x$-axis where $y = 0$, at $T = (-at^2, 0)$. Then $FT = a + at^2$. Also $FP$ equals the distance from $P$ to the directrix $x = -a$, which is $at^2 + a$. So triangle $FTP$ is isosceles with $FT = FP$, and its base angles at $T$ and $P$ are equal.

The horizontal line through $P$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, so the angle it makes with the tangent equals the angle at $T$ between the tangent and the $x$-axis (corresponding angles). That angle equals the angle at $P$ between the tangent and $PF$. So a ray arriving parallel to the axis is reflected along $PF$, through the focus.

blocks.title: Foci and tangents of an ellipse
blocks.body: Prove that for any tangent line to the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ (with $a > b > 0$), the product of the distances from the two foci to the line equals $b^2$.
blocks.solution:
The tangent at $(x_0, y_0)$ is $\frac{x_0}{a^2}x + \frac{y_0}{b^2}y - 1 = 0$. Write $N = \frac{x_0^2}{a^4} + \frac{y_0^2}{b^4}$. The distances from $(\pm c, 0)$ are $\frac{|\pm c x_0/a^2 - 1|}{\sqrt N}$, so their product is
$$\frac{\left|\frac{c^2 x_0^2}{a^4} - 1\right|}{N} = \frac{1 - \frac{c^2 x_0^2}{a^4}}{N},$$
since $|x_0| \le a$ and $c < a$ make $\frac{c^2x_0^2}{a^4} < 1$. Now compute $b^2 N$, using $\frac{y_0^2}{b^2} = 1 - \frac{x_0^2}{a^2}$ and $b^2 - a^2 = -c^2$:
$$b^2 N = \frac{b^2 x_0^2}{a^4} + 1 - \frac{x_0^2}{a^2} = 1 + \frac{(b^2 - a^2)x_0^2}{a^4} = 1 - \frac{c^2 x_0^2}{a^4}.$$
So the product is $b^2$, the same for every tangent.

blocks.body:
- For an ellipse $c^2 = a^2 - b^2$, for a hyperbola $c^2 = a^2 + b^2$. Mixing them up is the most common error.
- In $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ the major axis is along $x$ only if $a > b$; if $b > a$ the foci are on the $y$-axis.
- The discriminant test assumes the curve is non-degenerate: $x^2 + 2y^2 + 1 = 0$ passes the ellipse test but is empty.
- A circle is an ellipse with $e = 0$, but it has no directrix; the focus–directrix definition covers only $e > 0$.
- Asymptotes are not part of a hyperbola, and a parabola has none: its distance from any fixed line grows without bound as you move along it.

Polar and parametric descriptions of conics are developed in [[parametric-polar]], and the rotation that removes the $xy$ term is a special case of [[diagonalization]] of a symmetric matrix, as in the [[spectral-theorem]]. Points with rational coordinates on the unit circle come from lines of rational slope through $(-1, 0)$, which is how [[pythagorean]] triples are found; on a cubic curve the same idea leads to [[elliptic-curves]]. Conics are the first examples of plane [[curves]].

entry.sum: Area and volume measure how much room a plane figure or a solid takes up, in square or cubic units. Almost every school formula comes from three ideas: cutting and rearranging, comparing cross-sections (Cavalieri's principle), and scaling, under which lengths multiply by $k$, areas by $k^2$ and volumes by $k^3$.
key: V_{\text{prism}} = Ah,\qquad V_{\text{pyramid, cone}} = \tfrac13 Ah,\qquad V_{\text{sphere}} = \tfrac43\pi r^3,\qquad S_{\text{sphere}} = 4\pi r^2
entry.why: Measuring land, material, capacity and cost all need these formulas, and the scaling law explains everyday facts such as why large animals need thick legs and why small objects cool faster.

links.note: Lebesgue measure makes length, area and volume precise for very general sets, and the Banach–Tarski paradox shows that some sets cannot be given a volume compatible with rigid motions.
The number of lattice points inside a circle of radius $r$ is about $\pi r^2$, and estimating the error in this approximation is the Gauss circle problem.

refs: Kiselev, Kiselev's Geometry, Book II: Stereometry

blocks.body:
How much paint covers a wall, how much water fills a tank, how much land is in a field? Area and volume answer these, and the formulas are familiar. Less familiar is why they are true: why a cone holds exactly a third of the cylinder around it, or why the surface of a ball is $4\pi r^2$.

This page builds the standard formulas from three ideas, cut-and-rearrange, cross-sections and scaling, using facts about triangles from [[euclid-basics]] and circles from [[circles]]. At the end we see how calculus computes areas and volumes, and why a fully precise notion of volume is subtler than it looks.

blocks.title: Area by cutting and rearranging
blocks.body:
Area is measured in unit squares, and an $a \times b$ rectangle holds $ab$ of them (exactly when $a, b$ are whole numbers, and by approximation in general). Two rules then do most of the work: congruent figures have equal area, and if a figure is cut into pieces, its area is the sum of their areas.

- Parallelogram: cut a right triangle off one end and slide it to the other; you get a rectangle with the same base $b$ and height $h$. Area $bh$.
- Triangle: two copies of a triangle fit together into a parallelogram, so its area is $\frac12 bh$. If two sides $a, b$ meet at angle $C$, the height onto $b$ is $a\sin C$, so the area is $\frac12 ab\sin C$.
- Trapezium with parallel sides $a, b$ and height $h$: two copies, one turned upside down, form a parallelogram with base $a + b$. Area $\frac12 (a+b)h$.

Every polygon can be cut into triangles, so these rules give the area of any polygon.

blocks.title: Circles and radians
blocks.body:
All circles are similar, so the ratio of circumference to diameter is the same for all of them; this constant is $\pi \approx 3.14159$. A circle of radius $r$ has circumference $2\pi r$.

For the area, cut the disc into many thin sectors like slices of a pizza and lay them side by side, alternately pointing up and down. The result is nearly a parallelogram whose height is $r$ and whose base is half the circumference, $\pi r$. As the slices get thinner the approximation becomes perfect, giving area $\pi r^2$.

An angle $\theta$ in radians is the arc length it cuts off on a circle of radius 1; a full turn is $2\pi$. On a circle of radius $r$, an angle $\theta$ at the centre cuts off an arc of length $r\theta$ and a sector of area $\frac{\theta}{2\pi}\cdot \pi r^2 = \frac12 r^2\theta$. These formulas are the main reason radians are used: in degrees they carry an awkward factor $\frac{\pi}{180}$.

blocks.title: Scaling law
blocks.body: If a figure is enlarged by scale factor $k > 0$ (every length multiplied by $k$), its area is multiplied by $k^2$. If a solid is enlarged by scale factor $k$, its surface area is multiplied by $k^2$ and its volume by $k^3$.

blocks.title: Why
blocks.body: A unit square becomes a $k \times k$ square, of area $k^2$; a unit cube becomes a $k \times k \times k$ cube, of volume $k^3$. A rectangle or box built from such units scales the same way. A general shape can be approximated from inside and outside by unions of tiny squares (or cubes); enlarging the shape enlarges each tiny square, multiplying every approximation by $k^2$ (or $k^3$), so it multiplies the area (or volume) too. For triangles you can also see it directly: base and height both get multiplied by $k$, so $\frac12 bh$ gets multiplied by $k^2$.

blocks.title: Volume and Cavalieri's principle
blocks.body:
A box $a \times b \times c$ holds $abc$ unit cubes. A prism or cylinder is a base of area $A$ moved straight up through height $h$, and its volume is $Ah$: think of it as a stack of thin identical slices.

Now imagine a stack of coins. Push it so that it leans; its shape changes, but every coin is still there, so the volume does not change. This is the idea behind Cavalieri's principle: if two solids lie between the same two parallel planes, and every plane parallel to them cuts both solids in cross-sections of equal area, then the solids have equal volume. In particular a slanted prism or cylinder with base area $A$ and perpendicular height $h$ still has volume $Ah$. At school the principle is taken as a basic fact; with calculus it becomes the formula $V = \int A(z)\,dz$, where $A(z)$ is the area of the cross-section at height $z$.

blocks.title: Pyramids and cones
blocks.body: A pyramid or cone with base area $A$ and perpendicular height $h$ has volume $\frac13 Ah$. In particular a circular cone of radius $r$ has volume $\frac13\pi r^2 h$.

Step 1: a special pyramid. Take a cube of side $a$ and a vertex $O$ of it. The three faces of the cube not containing $O$ are bases of three square pyramids with apex $O$, each of height $a$, and these three pyramids are congruent and fill the cube. So each has volume $\frac13 a^3 = \frac13 (a^2)(a)$.

Step 2: any height. Stretching that pyramid vertically by a factor $\frac{h}{a}$ multiplies every horizontal slice's thickness, and hence the volume, by $\frac{h}{a}$. So a pyramid on an $a \times a$ square with its apex above a corner and height $h$ has volume $\frac13 a^2 h$.

Step 3: any base. Cut a pyramid or cone with base area $A$ and height $h$ by a plane parallel to the base at height $z$. The section is a copy of the base shrunk towards the apex by the factor $\frac{h - z}{h}$, so its area is $A\left(\frac{h-z}{h}\right)^2$ by the scaling law. This depends only on $A$, $h$ and $z$, not on the shape of the base or where the apex sits. By Cavalieri's principle, all pyramids and cones with base area $A$ and height $h$ have the same volume as the square pyramid of Step 2 with $a^2 = A$, which is $\frac13 Ah$.

With calculus the same cross-sections give it in one line: $\int_0^h A\left(1 - \frac{z}{h}\right)^2 dz = \frac13 Ah$.

blocks.title: The sphere (Archimedes)
blocks.body: A ball of radius $r$ has volume $\frac43 \pi r^3$ and its surface has area $4\pi r^2$.

Compare a hemisphere of radius $r$ with a cylinder of radius $r$ and height $r$ from which a cone has been removed: the cone has its base on the top of the cylinder and its apex at the centre of the bottom. Stand both on a table.

At height $z$ (with $0 \le z \le r$), the hemisphere's cross-section is a disc of radius $\sqrt{r^2 - z^2}$ by Pythagoras, so its area is $\pi(r^2 - z^2)$. The other solid's cross-section is a ring: the cylinder gives a disc of radius $r$, and the cone, whose radius grows from 0 at the bottom to $r$ at the top, removes a disc of radius $z$. Its area is $\pi r^2 - \pi z^2$. The areas agree at every height, so by Cavalieri's principle the volumes agree:
$$V_{\text{hemisphere}} = \pi r^2 \cdot r - \tfrac13 \pi r^2 \cdot r = \tfrac23 \pi r^3,$$
and the whole ball has volume $\frac43\pi r^3$.

For the surface, think of a thin shell between radii $r$ and $r + \delta$. Its volume is $\frac43\pi (r+\delta)^3 - \frac43 \pi r^3 = 4\pi r^2 \delta + 4\pi r\delta^2 + \frac43\pi\delta^3$, and it is also approximately (surface area) $\times\, \delta$. Dividing by $\delta$ and letting $\delta \to 0$ gives surface area $4\pi r^2$, the derivative of the volume.

blocks.title: Surfaces, calculus and what volume really is
blocks.body:
Other curved surfaces can be unrolled. A cylinder's side unrolls into a rectangle $2\pi r$ by $h$, area $2\pi rh$. A cone's side, with slant height $l$, unrolls into a sector of radius $l$ whose arc is $2\pi r$; a sector's area is half its radius times its arc, so the area is $\frac12 \cdot l \cdot 2\pi r = \pi rl$. A sphere cannot be unrolled flat without stretching, which is why we used the shell argument.

Calculus turns Cavalieri's principle into a general method; see [[integral-applications]]. Rotating the graph of $y = f(x)$, $a \le x \le b$, about the $x$-axis sweeps out a solid whose cross-sections are discs of area $\pi f(x)^2$, so its volume is $\pi\int_a^b f(x)^2\,dx$. With $f(x) = \sqrt{r^2 - x^2}$ on $[-r, r]$ this gives $\pi\left[r^2 x - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-r}^{r} = \frac43\pi r^3$ again.

What is area, precisely? For polygons, the Wallace–Bolyai–Gerwien theorem says two polygons of equal area can always be cut into finitely many pieces that rearrange from one to the other. In space this fails: soon after Hilbert posed the question in 1900 as his third problem, Dehn proved that some polyhedra of equal volume cannot be cut into matching polyhedral pieces; a cube and a regular tetrahedron of the same volume are an example. So volume genuinely needs limits. For wild sets even limits are not enough: the Banach–Tarski paradox cuts a ball into five pieces that reassemble, by rotations and translations, into two balls of the original size. Those pieces cannot be assigned any volume, and [[lebesgue]] measure explains which sets do.

blocks.title: A segment of a circle
blocks.body: A chord cuts off an arc of a circle of radius 6 subtending an angle of $60^\circ$ at the centre. Find the area of the smaller region between the chord and the arc.
blocks.solution: In radians the angle is $\frac{\pi}{3}$. The sector has area $\frac12 \cdot 6^2 \cdot \frac{\pi}{3} = 6\pi$. The triangle formed by the chord and the two radii has area $\frac12 \cdot 6 \cdot 6 \cdot \sin 60^\circ = 9\sqrt3$. The segment is the difference: $6\pi - 9\sqrt3 \approx 3.26$.

blocks.title: The frustum
blocks.body: A lampshade is a cone with its top cut off by a plane parallel to the base: a frustum with base radius $R$, top radius $r < R$ and height $h$. Show that its volume is $\frac13\pi h(R^2 + Rr + r^2)$, and evaluate it for $R = 3$, $r = 1$, $h = 4$.
blocks.solution:
Complete the frustum to a cone of height $H$. The small cone that was cut off has height $H - h$ and is similar to the big one, so $\frac{r}{H - h} = \frac{R}{H}$. Solving, $H = \frac{hR}{R - r}$ and $H - h = \frac{hr}{R - r}$. The frustum's volume is
$$\frac13\pi R^2 H - \frac13 \pi r^2 (H - h) = \frac{\pi h}{3}\cdot\frac{R^3 - r^3}{R - r} = \frac{\pi h}{3}(R^2 + Rr + r^2),$$
using $R^3 - r^3 = (R - r)(R^2 + Rr + r^2)$. For $R = 3$, $r = 1$, $h = 4$: $\frac{4\pi}{3}(9 + 3 + 1) = \frac{52\pi}{3}$.

Check the extremes: $r = R$ gives $\pi R^2 h$, a cylinder; $r = 0$ gives $\frac13\pi R^2 h$, a cone.

blocks.title: A tetrahedron inside a cube
blocks.body: Find the volume of a regular tetrahedron with edge $a$, without using any formula for the height of a tetrahedron.
blocks.solution:
In a cube of side $s$, choose four vertices no two of which share an edge, for example $(0,0,0)$, $(s,s,0)$, $(s,0,s)$, $(0,s,s)$. Each pair is joined by a diagonal of a face, of length $s\sqrt2$, so these four points form a regular tetrahedron with edge $s\sqrt2$.

The cube minus the tetrahedron consists of four corner pieces. Each is a tetrahedron with three mutually perpendicular edges of length $s$ meeting at a cube vertex: a pyramid with right-triangle base of area $\frac12 s^2$ and height $s$, so of volume $\frac16 s^3$. Therefore the regular tetrahedron has volume $s^3 - 4\cdot\frac16 s^3 = \frac13 s^3$.

With $a = s\sqrt2$, that is $s = \frac{a}{\sqrt2}$, the volume is $\frac13\cdot\frac{a^3}{2\sqrt2} = \frac{a^3}{6\sqrt2} = \frac{\sqrt2}{12}a^3$.

blocks.title: Half full?
blocks.body: A conical glass, point downwards, is filled with water to half its height. What fraction of the glass's volume is water?
blocks.solution: The water itself forms a cone similar to the glass with scale factor $\frac12$. By the scaling law its volume is $\left(\frac12\right)^3 = \frac18$ of the glass's. A glass filled to half its height holds only one eighth of its capacity; to be half full by volume the water must reach $\left(\frac12\right)^{1/3} \approx 0.79$ of the height.

blocks.body:
- Area scales by $k^2$ and volume by $k^3$, not by $k$. A model at scale $1:50$ has $\frac{1}{2500}$ of the area and $\frac{1}{125000}$ of the volume.
- The sector and arc formulas $\frac12 r^2\theta$ and $r\theta$ need $\theta$ in radians.
- In $\frac13\pi r^2 h$ the height $h$ is perpendicular, not the slant height $l$; the slant height appears in the curved surface area $\pi rl$, and $l^2 = r^2 + h^2$.
- Equal perimeters do not mean equal areas: a $1 \times 9$ and a $5 \times 5$ rectangle both have perimeter 20, but areas 9 and 25.
- Do not mix units: $1\ \text{m}^2 = 10^4\ \text{cm}^2$ and $1\ \text{m}^3 = 10^6\ \text{cm}^3$.

The coordinate geometry of solids is in [[solid-geometry]]. The limits hidden in the circle and sphere arguments are made rigorous by the [[riemann-integral]], and [[multiple-integrals]] compute volumes of regions bounded by any surfaces. The general theory of length, area and volume is [[lebesgue]] measure. Area appears in number theory too: counting lattice points in a large disc is a question about [[floor-functions]] whose answer starts with $\pi r^2$.

1. Show that a sphere has two thirds of the volume, and two thirds of the total surface area, of the smallest cylinder containing it.
2. Two similar bottles have heights 20 cm and 30 cm. The smaller holds 400 ml. How much does the larger hold?
3. Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating $y = \sqrt x$, $0 \le x \le 4$, about the $x$-axis.
4. A square pyramid has all eight edges of length 2. Find its height and volume.

entry.sum: Solid geometry studies points, lines, planes and solids in three-dimensional space: how lines and planes can sit relative to each other (in space two lines may be skew, neither meeting nor parallel), how to measure the angles and distances between them, and the shapes of polyhedra. With coordinates, a plane is a single linear equation $ax+by+cz=d$ whose coefficients form a normal vector, and most measurements reduce to dot and cross products.
key: \operatorname{dist}(\ell_1,\ell_2)=\frac{|(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)\cdot(\mathbf d_1\times\mathbf d_2)|}{|\mathbf d_1\times\mathbf d_2|}\quad(\ell_1:\mathbf a+t\mathbf d_1,\ \ell_2:\mathbf b+s\mathbf d_2 \text{ skew})
entry.why: Engineering drawings, navigation, crystallography and 3D computer graphics all need angles and distances between lines and planes, and space is where the intuition for linear algebra in more than two dimensions is first built.

links.note: Euler's formula $V-E+F=2$ is the first instance of the Euler characteristic, a topological invariant that distinguishes the sphere from the torus and other surfaces.
3D graphics and ray tracing rely on ray–plane intersections, normal vectors for lighting and back-face culling, and projections from space onto the screen plane.

refs: Kiselev, Kiselev's Geometry, Book II: Stereometry
aliases: distance from a point to a plane

blocks.body:
Look at the edges of a room. The line where the floor meets the front wall and the vertical line in a back corner never meet, yet they are not parallel either. Such lines are called skew, and they cannot occur in a plane. Space has more room than the plane, and that is the source of both the new phenomena and the new questions: how far apart are two skew lines? At what angle does a staircase rise from the floor? How many kinds of perfectly symmetric solid are there?

This page answers such questions in two ways, by classical arguments with triangles from [[euclid-basics]] and by vectors from [[vectors-plane]]. Each method makes some problems easy; it pays to have both.

blocks.title: How lines and planes can meet
blocks.body:
Three facts set the rules. Two distinct points lie on exactly one line. Three points not on a line lie on exactly one plane (a camera tripod never wobbles). If two points of a line lie in a plane, the whole line does.

From these one gets the possible positions:

- Two lines either meet in one point, are parallel (lie in a common plane and do not meet), or are skew (lie in no common plane).
- A line and a plane either meet in one point, are parallel (do not meet), or the line lies in the plane.
- Two distinct planes either are parallel or meet in a line.

So a plane is fixed by three non-collinear points, by a line and a point off it, by two meeting lines, or by two parallel lines.

The angle between two skew lines is defined by moving one of them parallel to itself until the two meet, and taking the angle (at most $90^\circ$) between them. On a cube, an edge of the top face and a non-parallel edge of the bottom face are skew and at $90^\circ$.

blocks.title: Perpendicular to a plane; angles with planes
blocks.body:
A line is perpendicular to a plane if it meets the plane and is perpendicular to every line in the plane through the meeting point (its foot). The orthogonal projection of a point $P$ onto a plane is the foot of the perpendicular from $P$.

The angle between a line and a plane it meets (not perpendicularly) is the angle between the line and its projection onto the plane. The angle between two planes meeting in a line $m$ (the dihedral angle) is measured by choosing a point on $m$ and drawing, in each plane, the line through that point perpendicular to $m$; it is the angle between these two lines.

blocks.title: Test for perpendicularity
blocks.body: If a line is perpendicular to two intersecting lines of a plane at their common point, it is perpendicular to the plane.

Let the line have direction vector $\mathbf n$ and the two lines of the plane have directions $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$, not parallel. Every line in the plane through the common point has a direction of the form $\lambda\mathbf u + \mu\mathbf v$. Then $\mathbf n \cdot (\lambda\mathbf u + \mu\mathbf v) = \lambda(\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf u) + \mu(\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf v) = 0$, so the line is perpendicular to all of them.

blocks.title: Theorem of three perpendiculars
blocks.body: Let $P$ be a point outside a plane $\Pi$, let $O$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $\Pi$, and let $\ell$ be a line in $\Pi$ through a point $Q \ne O$. Then $PQ \perp \ell$ if and only if $OQ \perp \ell$.

Let $\mathbf d$ be a direction vector of $\ell$. Since $\overrightarrow{PQ} = \overrightarrow{PO} + \overrightarrow{OQ}$ and $\overrightarrow{PO}$ is perpendicular to the plane, hence to $\mathbf d$, we get $\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\mathbf d = \overrightarrow{OQ}\cdot\mathbf d$. One is zero exactly when the other is.

This is the standard way to find a dihedral angle by hand: drop a perpendicular from a point of one plane to the other, then draw from its foot the perpendicular to the common line.

blocks.title: Coordinates: lines and planes as equations
blocks.body:
With three perpendicular axes, a point is $(x, y, z)$. Pythagoras used twice gives the distance between $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2,z_2)$ as $\sqrt{(x_1-x_2)^2+(y_1-y_2)^2+(z_1-z_2)^2}$, and so the sphere with centre $(p,q,r)$ and radius $R$ is $(x-p)^2+(y-q)^2+(z-r)^2 = R^2$.

A line through the point with position vector $\mathbf a$ with direction $\mathbf d$ is $\mathbf r = \mathbf a + t\mathbf d$. A plane is best described by a normal vector $\mathbf n = (a, b, c)$ perpendicular to it: a point $\mathbf r$ lies in the plane through $\mathbf r_0$ exactly when $\mathbf n\cdot(\mathbf r - \mathbf r_0) = 0$, which expands to one linear equation
$$ax + by + cz = d, \qquad d = \mathbf n\cdot\mathbf r_0.$$
Given three points $A, B, C$ of the plane, a normal is the cross product $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}$.

Angles now become dot products. Between two lines with directions $\mathbf d_1, \mathbf d_2$: $\cos\theta = \frac{|\mathbf d_1\cdot\mathbf d_2|}{|\mathbf d_1||\mathbf d_2|}$. Between two planes: the same formula with their normals. Between a line and a plane: $\sin\phi = \frac{|\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf d||\mathbf n|}$, since the line makes angle $90^\circ - \phi$ with the normal.

blocks.title: Distance from a point to a plane
blocks.body:
The distance from $P_0 = (x_0, y_0, z_0)$ to the plane $ax + by + cz = d$ is
$$\frac{|ax_0 + by_0 + cz_0 - d|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}}.$$

Let $\mathbf n = (a,b,c)$. The perpendicular from $P_0$ is the line $\mathbf r = \mathbf p_0 + t\mathbf n$, and it meets the plane when $\mathbf n\cdot(\mathbf p_0 + t\mathbf n) = d$, that is at $t = \frac{d - \mathbf n\cdot\mathbf p_0}{|\mathbf n|^2}$. The foot is at distance $|t||\mathbf n| = \frac{|\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf p_0 - d|}{|\mathbf n|}$ from $P_0$, which is the formula. Any other point of the plane is farther away, by Pythagoras in the right triangle it forms with $P_0$ and the foot.

For two skew lines $\mathbf a + t\mathbf d_1$ and $\mathbf b + s\mathbf d_2$, the same idea works: $\mathbf n = \mathbf d_1\times\mathbf d_2$ is perpendicular to both, and the plane through the second line with normal $\mathbf n$ is parallel to the first line. The distance between the lines is the distance from $\mathbf a$ to that plane, $\frac{|(\mathbf b - \mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf n|}$.

blocks.title: Projections and areas
blocks.body:
Project a flat figure of area $S$ orthogonally onto a plane making angle $\theta$ with the figure's plane. Lengths along the common line direction are unchanged, while lengths perpendicular to it shrink by the factor $\cos\theta$. A rectangle with one side along that direction therefore has its area multiplied by $\cos\theta$, and approximating any figure by such rectangles gives
$$S' = S\cos\theta.$$
This is often the quickest way to find a dihedral angle: compute an area and the area of its shadow.

blocks.title: Polyhedra and Euler's formula
blocks.body:
A polyhedron is a solid bounded by flat polygonal faces. Count its vertices $V$, edges $E$ and faces $F$: a cube has $8, 12, 6$; a square pyramid $5, 8, 5$; a triangular prism $6, 9, 5$. In each case $V - E + F = 2$, and Euler's formula says this holds for every convex polyhedron. (A proof sketch: remove one face and stretch the rest flat in the plane; the removed face becomes the unbounded region around the drawing. Now delete edges one at a time: while there is a cycle, delete an edge on it, which merges the two regions on its sides; when no cycle is left the drawing is a tree, and deleting an edge to a vertex of degree 1 removes that vertex too. Either way $V - E + F$ is unchanged, and at the end a single vertex and one region remain, giving $1 - 0 + 1 = 2$. The plane version is developed in [[planar-graphs]].)

A polyhedron is regular, or Platonic, if all faces are congruent regular polygons and the same number of faces meet at every vertex, with the solid convex. There are exactly five: the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron and icosahedron. The example below proves there can be no others.

blocks.title: Angles in a cube
blocks.body: In the unit cube with vertices $(0,0,0)$ to $(1,1,1)$, find: (a) the angle between the space diagonal from $O = (0,0,0)$ to $(1,1,1)$ and the bottom face; (b) the angle between the face diagonals from $O$ to $(1,1,0)$ and to $(1,0,1)$; (c) the angle between the plane through $(1,0,0)$, $(0,1,0)$, $(0,0,1)$ and the bottom face.
blocks.solution:
(a) The bottom face $z = 0$ has normal $(0,0,1)$ and the diagonal has direction $(1,1,1)$. So $\sin\phi = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}$ and $\phi \approx 35.26^\circ$. Classically: the projection of the diagonal is the bottom diagonal of length $\sqrt2$, and the height is 1, so $\tan\phi = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}$, the same angle.

(b) $\cos\theta = \frac{(1,1,0)\cdot(1,0,1)}{\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2} = \frac12$, so $\theta = 60^\circ$. Without vectors: the three points $(1,1,0)$, $(1,0,1)$ and $O$ are joined by face diagonals, all of length $\sqrt2$, so they form an equilateral triangle.

(c) The plane is $x + y + z = 1$ with normal $(1,1,1)$; the bottom has normal $(0,0,1)$. So $\cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}$, $\theta \approx 54.74^\circ$. Check by projection: the triangle has three sides $\sqrt2$, so its area is $\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\cdot 2 = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}$. Its shadow on the bottom is the right triangle with vertices $(1,0,0)$, $(0,1,0)$, $(0,0,0)$, of area $\frac12$. Indeed $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt3} = \frac12$.

blocks.title: Distance between skew lines
blocks.body: In the same cube, find the distance between the space diagonal through $(0,0,0)$ and $(1,1,1)$ and the face diagonal through $(1,0,0)$ and $(0,1,0)$.
blocks.solution:
The lines are $\ell_1: t(1,1,1)$ and $\ell_2: (1,0,0) + s(-1,1,0)$. They are skew: points of $\ell_2$ have $z = 0$, so a common point would have $t = 0$, which is the origin, and the origin is not on $\ell_2$ (it would need $1 - s = 0$ and $s = 0$); and the directions are not parallel.

Take $\mathbf n = (1,1,1)\times(-1,1,0) = (-1, -1, 2)$, with $|\mathbf n| = \sqrt6$. The vector joining the base points is $(1,0,0) - (0,0,0) = (1,0,0)$, and $(1,0,0)\cdot\mathbf n = -1$. So the distance is $\frac{1}{\sqrt6} \approx 0.408$.

Note also that $(1,1,1)\cdot(-1,1,0) = 0$: these skew lines are perpendicular.

blocks.title: Why only five regular solids
blocks.body: Prove that a convex regular polyhedron has faces that are triangles, squares or pentagons, and that there are at most five possible combinations of face type and number of faces at a vertex.
blocks.solution:
Let each face be a regular $p$-gon and let $q$ faces meet at each vertex, with $p, q \ge 3$ (a corner needs at least three faces). The angle of a regular $p$-gon is $\frac{(p-2)\cdot 180^\circ}{p}$. At a convex corner the face angles add up to less than $360^\circ$ (if they added up to exactly $360^\circ$ the corner would be flat). So
$$q\cdot\frac{(p-2)180^\circ}{p} < 360^\circ \iff q(p-2) < 2p \iff (p-2)(q-2) < 4.$$
With $p - 2, q - 2 \ge 1$, the only possibilities are $(p,q) = (3,3), (3,4), (4,3), (3,5), (5,3)$. These are the tetrahedron, octahedron, cube, icosahedron and dodecahedron, and each of them exists.

Euler's formula then gives the counts. Each edge lies on two faces and joins two vertices, so $pF = 2E = qV$. Substituting into $V - E + F = 2$ gives $\frac1p + \frac1q = \frac12 + \frac1E$. For the dodecahedron, $(p,q) = (5,3)$: $\frac15 + \frac13 - \frac12 = \frac1{30}$, so $E = 30$, $F = 12$, $V = 20$.

blocks.body:
- Two lines that do not meet need not be parallel: in space they may be skew.
- A line perpendicular to one line of a plane need not be perpendicular to the plane; it must be perpendicular to two intersecting lines of the plane.
- The angle between a line and a plane uses the sine of the angle with the normal, not the cosine: $\sin\phi = \frac{|\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf d||\mathbf n|}$.
- The angle between planes is the angle between their normals or its supplement; take absolute values to get the angle between $0^\circ$ and $90^\circ$.
- The equation $ax + by + cz = d$ is a plane, not a line; a line in space needs two such equations, or a parametric form.

Volumes and surface areas of solids are on [[area-volume]]. The coordinate methods are three-dimensional [[analytic-geometry]], and the volume of the box spanned by three vectors is the absolute value of a [[determinants|determinant]], the triple product $\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c)$. Euler's formula is proved for plane drawings in [[planar-graphs]] and becomes the Euler characteristic in [[classification-of-surfaces]]. Packing and covering questions about solids belong to [[discrete-geometry]].

2. In a regular tetrahedron, show that two opposite edges are perpendicular.
3. Show that the dihedral angle of a regular tetrahedron is $\arccos\frac13 \approx 70.5^\circ$.
4. A regular square pyramid has all edges of length 2. Find the angle between a lateral edge and the base.
