entry.sum: A straightedge-and-compass construction builds new points from given ones using only two moves: draw the line through two points, and draw the circle with a given centre through a given point. Starting from a unit length, the lengths one can build are exactly those obtained from rational numbers by $+,-,\times,\div$ and square roots, so every constructible number has degree a power of 2 over $\mathbb{Q}$; this is why the cube cannot be doubled nor a general angle trisected.
key: x \text{ constructible} \iff x \in K_n \text{ for a tower } \mathbb{Q}=K_0\subset K_1\subset\cdots\subset K_n\subset\mathbb{R},\ K_{i}=K_{i-1}(\sqrt{d_i}),\ d_i \in K_{i-1},\ d_i>0
\text{regular } n\text{-gon } (n\ge 3) \text{ constructible} \iff n = 2^k p_1\cdots p_r,\ p_i \text{ distinct Fermat primes}
entry.why: Constructions are where many students first meet proofs that something is impossible, and the solution of the three classical problems of antiquity (doubling the cube, trisecting the angle, squaring the circle) is one of the first great successes of field theory.

links.note: By the Gauss–Wantzel theorem a regular $p$-gon with $p$ prime is constructible exactly when $p$ is a Fermat prime $2^{2^k}+1$, and only five Fermat primes (3, 5, 17, 257, 65537) are known.

blocks.body:
Euclid's geometry is built with two idealised tools: a straightedge, with no marks on it, for drawing the line through two points, and a compass for drawing a circle with a given centre passing through a given point. With them you can bisect any angle, draw perpendiculars and parallels, and build regular triangles, squares, pentagons and hexagons. Three problems resisted for over two thousand years: construct a cube with twice the volume of a given cube; divide any angle into three equal parts; construct a square with the same area as a given circle.

All three are impossible, and the reason is algebraic. This page first shows what the tools can do, with proofs by congruent triangles from [[euclid-basics]] and power of a point from [[circles]], and then turns constructions into algebra using [[fields-ext]].

blocks.title: The basic constructions
blocks.body:
Each construction comes with a reason it works.

1. Perpendicular bisector of $AB$. Draw the circle centred $A$ through $B$ and the circle centred $B$ through $A$; they meet at $X$ and $Y$. Then $XA = XB$ and $YA = YB$, and the points equidistant from $A$ and $B$ form the perpendicular bisector, so the line $XY$ is it. It also gives the midpoint of $AB$.
2. Bisecting angle $\angle AOB$. The circle centred $O$ through $A$ meets ray $OB$ at $B'$. Construct the perpendicular bisector of $AB'$; it passes through $O$ (since $OA = OB'$), and by symmetry it bisects the angle.
3. Perpendicular to a line $\ell$ through a point $P$. Draw a circle centred $P$ meeting $\ell$ at two points; their perpendicular bisector passes through $P$ and is perpendicular to $\ell$.
4. Parallel to $\ell$ through $P$. Draw the perpendicular $m$ to $\ell$ through $P$, then the perpendicular to $m$ through $P$.
5. Transferring a length. The compass as described collapses when lifted, but Euclid showed (his second proposition) that a length can still be copied to any point, so we may use the compass with a radius equal to any constructed distance.
6. Dividing $AB$ into $n$ equal parts. Mark $n$ equal steps along any ray from $A$, ending at $C_n$; join $C_n$ to $B$ and draw parallels through the other marks. By the intercept theorem they cut $AB$ into equal parts.

The equilateral triangle, the square and the regular hexagon follow directly (a hexagon is six radius-length chords around a circle).

blocks.title: From points to numbers
blocks.body:
Fix two points $(0,0)$ and $(1,0)$ to set the unit of length. Call a point constructible if it can be reached from these two by a finite sequence of lines and circles, each new point being an intersection of lines or circles already drawn. Call a real number $x$ constructible if the point $(x, 0)$ is.

Which numbers do we get? Lengths can be added and subtracted along a line by copying them. Products and quotients come from similar triangles: on one ray from $O$ mark $OU = 1$ and $OA = a$, on another ray mark $OB = b$; the parallel to $UB$ through $A$ meets the second ray at a point $C$ with $OC = ab$, because triangles $OUB$ and $OAC$ are similar. Swapping roles gives $b/a$.

Square roots come from a circle. Put $A$, $B$, $C$ on a line with $AB = a$ and $BC = 1$, draw the circle on diameter $AC$, and erect the perpendicular at $B$, meeting the circle at $D$. By power of a point (or similar triangles), $BD^2 = AB\cdot BC = a$, so $BD = \sqrt a$.

So starting from 1 we can reach every number built from integers by $+, -, \times, \div$ and $\sqrt{\ }$, such as $\sqrt{2 + \sqrt3} - \frac{1}{\sqrt5}$. The striking fact is that nothing else is reachable.

blocks.title: Characterisation of constructible numbers
blocks.body:
A real number $x$ is constructible if and only if there is a chain of fields
$$\mathbb{Q} = K_0 \subset K_1 \subset \cdots \subset K_n \subset \mathbb{R}, \qquad K_i = K_{i-1}(\sqrt{d_i}) \text{ with } d_i \in K_{i-1},\ d_i > 0,$$
such that $x \in K_n$. Consequently, if $x$ is constructible then $[\mathbb{Q}(x):\mathbb{Q}]$ is a power of 2.

The previous section shows the constructible numbers contain $\mathbb{Q}$ and are closed under the field operations and under square roots of positive numbers, so every element of such a $K_n$ is constructible.

For the converse, suppose every point drawn so far has both coordinates in a subfield $F$ of $\mathbb{R}$. A line through two such points has an equation $\alpha x + \beta y = \gamma$ with $\alpha, \beta, \gamma \in F$. A circle with centre $(p,q)$ through $(s,t)$ has equation $x^2 + y^2 - 2px - 2qy + c = 0$ with $c = 2ps + 2qt - s^2 - t^2 \in F$. Now look at the new intersection points.

- Two lines: solving two linear equations needs only $+, -, \times, \div$, so the intersection has coordinates in $F$.
- A line and a circle: solve the line's equation for one variable and substitute. This gives a quadratic equation with coefficients in $F$, whose roots lie in $F(\sqrt D)$, where $D \in F$ is its discriminant ($D \ge 0$ since the intersection is real). The other coordinate then also lies in $F(\sqrt D)$.
- Two circles: subtracting their equations removes $x^2 + y^2$ and leaves a linear equation, so the intersection points are those of a line and a circle.

So each new point has coordinates in $F$ or in $F(\sqrt D)$ for some positive $D \in F$. Starting with $F = \mathbb{Q}$ and following the construction step by step gives the required chain, and $x$, a coordinate of a constructed point, lies in its last field.

Finally each step has $[K_i : K_{i-1}] = 1$ or 2, so $[K_n : \mathbb{Q}] = 2^m$ by the tower law. Since $\mathbb{Q} \subseteq \mathbb{Q}(x) \subseteq K_n$, the degree $[\mathbb{Q}(x):\mathbb{Q}]$ divides $2^m$, so it is a power of 2.

blocks.title: The three classical problems
blocks.body:
Doubling the cube. A cube of side 1 has volume 1; doubling it needs side $\sqrt[3]2$. This number is a root of $x^3 - 2$, which has no rational roots (the only candidates are $\pm1$ and $\pm2$). A cubic with no rational root has no linear factor over $\mathbb{Q}$, so it is irreducible, and $[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]2):\mathbb{Q}] = 3$. This is not a power of 2, so $\sqrt[3]2$ is not constructible.

Trisecting the angle. Some angles can be trisected (a right angle, since $30^\circ$ is constructible), but not all. An angle $\theta$ can be drawn exactly when $\cos\theta$ is constructible (drop a perpendicular from a point of the unit circle). The $60^\circ$ angle is constructible, so it suffices to show $\cos 20^\circ$ is not. From $\cos3\theta = 4\cos^3\theta - 3\cos\theta$ with $\theta = 20^\circ$ we get $4c^3 - 3c = \frac12$, so $y = 2c$ satisfies $y^3 - 3y - 1 = 0$. The candidates $y = \pm 1$ fail ($1 - 3 - 1 = -3$ and $-1 + 3 - 1 = 1$), so this cubic is irreducible, $2\cos 20^\circ$ has degree 3, and $\cos20^\circ$ is not constructible.

Squaring the circle. A square of area $\pi$ has side $\sqrt\pi$; if it were constructible, so would be $\pi$, which would then be algebraic (a root of a nonzero polynomial with rational coefficients). Lindemann proved in 1882 that $\pi$ is transcendental, so this is impossible too. His proof is much harder and is not given here.

blocks.title: Regular polygons and a glimpse further
blocks.body:
A regular $n$-gon can be constructed exactly when the angle $\frac{2\pi}{n}$ can, that is, when $\cos\frac{2\pi}{n}$ is constructible. Gauss found in 1796 that the 17-gon is constructible, and the full answer (Gauss, with the converse completed by Wantzel in 1837) is: the regular $n$-gon is constructible if and only if $n = 2^k p_1 p_2 \cdots p_r$ where the $p_i$ are distinct Fermat primes, primes of the form $2^{2^j} + 1$. Only five are known: 3, 5, 17, 257, 65537; Euler showed $2^{32} + 1 = 641 \cdot 6700417$. For $3 \le n \le 20$ the constructible ones are $n = 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 15, 16, 17, 20$. The full proof uses [[galois]] theory and [[cyclotomic]] fields.

Other tools give other answers. The compass alone can construct every point that straightedge and compass can (Mohr–Mascheroni), and a straightedge with one given circle and its centre suffices too (Poncelet–Steiner). A marked ruler (a neusis construction, used by Archimedes) or paper folding can trisect angles and double the cube, because those tools can solve cubic equations.

blocks.title: The regular pentagon
blocks.body: Show that $\cos 72^\circ = \frac{\sqrt5 - 1}{4}$, and deduce that the regular pentagon is constructible.
blocks.solution:
Let $\theta = 72^\circ$ and $c = \cos\theta$. Since $5\theta = 360^\circ$, we have $3\theta = 360^\circ - 2\theta$, so $\cos3\theta = \cos2\theta$. Using $\cos3\theta = 4c^3 - 3c$ and $\cos2\theta = 2c^2 - 1$:
$$4c^3 - 2c^2 - 3c + 1 = 0, \qquad (c - 1)(4c^2 + 2c - 1) = 0.$$
Since $c \ne 1$, $c$ is a root of $4c^2 + 2c - 1 = 0$, and as $c > 0$, $c = \frac{-2 + \sqrt{20}}{8} = \frac{\sqrt5 - 1}{4}$.

This number is built from integers by a square root and field operations, so it is constructible: construct $\sqrt5$ as the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 1 and 2, subtract 1, and divide by 4. Then mark the point at that distance from the centre of a unit circle along a radius, erect the perpendicular there to cut the circle; the chord from it to the end of the radius is a side of the regular pentagon.

blocks.title: The regular heptagon is impossible
blocks.body: Show that $\alpha = 2\cos\frac{2\pi}{7}$ satisfies $\alpha^3 + \alpha^2 - 2\alpha - 1 = 0$, and deduce that the regular 7-gon cannot be constructed.
blocks.solution:
Let $\zeta = \cos\frac{2\pi}{7} + i\sin\frac{2\pi}{7}$ (see [[complex-numbers]]), so $\zeta^7 = 1$, $\zeta \ne 1$ and $\alpha = \zeta + \zeta^{-1}$. Since $\zeta^7 - 1 = (\zeta - 1)(\zeta^6 + \cdots + \zeta + 1)$, we get $1 + \zeta + \zeta^2 + \cdots + \zeta^6 = 0$. Dividing by $\zeta^3$:
$$(\zeta^3 + \zeta^{-3}) + (\zeta^2 + \zeta^{-2}) + (\zeta + \zeta^{-1}) + 1 = 0.$$
Now $\alpha^2 = \zeta^2 + \zeta^{-2} + 2$ and $\alpha^3 = \zeta^3 + \zeta^{-3} + 3\alpha$. Substituting, $(\alpha^3 - 3\alpha) + (\alpha^2 - 2) + \alpha + 1 = 0$, which is $\alpha^3 + \alpha^2 - 2\alpha - 1 = 0$.

The only possible rational roots are $\pm1$, giving $-1$ and $1$, not 0. So the cubic is irreducible, $[\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}] = 3$, and $\alpha$ is not constructible. Hence neither is $\cos\frac{2\pi}{7}$, and the heptagon cannot be constructed. This agrees with Gauss–Wantzel, since 7 is not a Fermat prime.

blocks.title: A square in a triangle
blocks.body: Given a triangle $ABC$ whose angles at $B$ and $C$ are acute, construct a square with two vertices on $BC$, one on $AB$ and one on $AC$.
blocks.solution:
Idea: draw a square with three of the four conditions, then enlarge it from $B$.

Choose any point $P$ on $AB$ between $A$ and $B$, and drop the perpendicular $PQ$ to $BC$. On $BC$, on the side of $Q$ away from $B$, mark $R$ with $QR = QP$, and complete the square $PQRS$ (perpendicular to $BC$ at $R$, of length $QP$). This square has $P$ on $AB$ and $Q, R$ on $BC$, but $S$ is probably not on $AC$.

Draw the line $BS$ and let it meet $AC$ at $S'$. The enlargement (homothety) with centre $B$ that sends $S$ to $S'$ maps lines through $B$ to themselves, so it sends $Q$ and $R$ to points of line $BC$ and $P$ to a point of line $AB$. It sends the square $PQRS$ to a square $P'Q'R'S'$, since enlargements preserve angles and multiply all lengths by the same factor. So $P'Q'R'S'$ has two vertices on $BC$, one on $AB$ and its fourth vertex $S'$ on $AC$, as required. (The acute angles ensure the square sits inside the triangle with $Q'$, $R'$ on the segment $BC$.)

Every step uses only perpendiculars, copied lengths and intersections, so it is a valid construction.

blocks.body:
- An impossibility proof is about exact constructions with finitely many steps. Approximate constructions, as accurate as you like, exist for everything.
- The marks matter: a straightedge with two marks on it is a different tool, and with it trisection is possible.
- The degree condition is necessary, not sufficient. Some numbers of degree 4 over $\mathbb{Q}$ are not constructible; the precise test is that the Galois group of the minimal polynomial has order a power of 2.
- Impossibility of trisection means no single method trisects every angle. Particular angles such as $90^\circ$ or $180^\circ$ can be trisected.
- A cubic with rational coefficients is irreducible exactly when it has no rational root, but for quartics and higher, having no rational root does not imply irreducibility: $(x^2 + 1)^2$ has no rational root.

The algebra behind this page is [[fields-ext]] and the tower law; the complete theory of which numbers and polygons are constructible is a chapter of [[galois]] theory, with the polygon question living in [[cyclotomic]] fields. The rational root test used here, and other irreducibility tests such as Eisenstein's criterion, are in [[integer-polynomials]] and [[polynomials-roots]]. The enlargement trick of the last example is a transformation in the sense of [[geo-transformations]].

3. Prove that the regular 9-gon is not constructible.
4. Given two segments of lengths $a$ and $b$, construct a segment of length $\sqrt{ab}$, the geometric mean.

entry.sum: For a prime $p$, the field $\mathbb{Q}_p$ of $p$-adic numbers is the completion of $\mathbb{Q}$ for the absolute value $|x|_p = p^{-v_p(x)}$, in which a number is small when it is divisible by a high power of $p$. Its elements are series $\sum_{i \ge n} a_i p^i$ with digits $0 \le a_i < p$ running infinitely to the left, and the $p$-adic integers $\mathbb{Z}_p = \{|x|_p \le 1\}$ package all congruences modulo $p, p^2, p^3, \dots$ into a single compact ring.
entry.why: Solving an equation in $\mathbb{Q}_p$ is the same as solving it modulo every power of $p$ at once, so p-adic numbers are the natural home for congruence arguments and for local-to-global principles such as the Hasse–Minkowski theorem; they are basic tools throughout modern number theory.

links.note: The ring $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is compact and totally disconnected, homeomorphic to the Cantor set, and $\mathbb{Q}_p$ is a standard example of a locally compact field with an ultrametric topology.

The construction of $\mathbb{Q}_p$ by Cauchy sequences is the same completion process that builds $\mathbb{R}$ from $\mathbb{Q}$, and by Ostrowski's theorem these completions are the only ones coming from absolute values on $\mathbb{Q}$.

refs: Koblitz, p-adic Numbers, p-adic Analysis, and Zeta-Functions

blocks.body:
Consider $1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + \cdots$. In the real numbers it diverges. But look at its partial sums $2^n - 1$: they are $\equiv -1$ modulo $2^n$, so modulo any fixed power of 2 they are eventually all equal to $-1$. If we decide that numbers divisible by a high power of 2 count as small, then $2^n \to 0$, and the series converges to $-1$, exactly as the formula $\frac{1}{1 - 2}$ for a geometric series predicts.

The $p$-adic numbers make this precise. They are built from $\mathbb{Q}$ using the [[p-adic-valuation]] as a measure of size, by the same completion process that builds $\mathbb{R}$ (see [[metric-spaces]]). The result is a number system in which congruences modulo $p, p^2, p^3, \dots$ become a single equation, and [[hensel]]'s lemma becomes a statement about convergence.

blocks.title: Measuring size by divisibility
blocks.body:
For a prime $p$ and a nonzero rational $x = p^n \frac{a}{b}$ with $p \nmid a$, $p \nmid b$, the $p$-adic valuation is $v_p(x) = n$ and the $p$-adic absolute value is $|x|_p = p^{-n}$; set $|0|_p = 0$. So $|24|_2 = \frac18$, $|\frac{1}{12}|_2 = 4$, $|7|_2 = 1$ and $|p^n|_p = p^{-n} \to 0$.

It is multiplicative, $|xy|_p = |x|_p|y|_p$, because valuations add. It satisfies a strong form of the triangle inequality,
$$|x + y|_p \le \max(|x|_p, |y|_p),$$
because if $p^n$ divides both $x$ and $y$ (in the sense of valuations), it divides $x + y$. An absolute value with this property is called non-Archimedean, or ultrametric. The distance $d(x,y) = |x - y|_p$ makes $\mathbb{Q}$ a metric space, but $\mathbb{Q}$ is not complete for it. For instance, for $p = 5$ there are integers $x_1 = 2, x_2 = 7, x_3 = 57, \dots$ with $x_n^2 \equiv -1 \pmod{5^n}$ and $x_{n+1} \equiv x_n \pmod{5^n}$ (by [[hensel]]'s lemma; see the example below). They form a Cauchy sequence, but a rational limit $r$ would satisfy $|r^2 + 1|_5 = \lim |x_n^2 + 1|_5 = 0$, that is $r^2 = -1$, which is impossible.

blocks.title: Strict triangle inequality
blocks.body: In any field with an ultrametric absolute value, if $|x| \ne |y|$ then $|x + y| = \max(|x|, |y|)$. More generally, if $|x_1| > |x_i|$ for all $i = 2, \dots, n$, then $|x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n| = |x_1|$.

Say $|x| > |y|$. Then $|x + y| \le |x|$. Also $x = (x + y) + (-y)$, so $|x| \le \max(|x + y|, |y|)$; since $|x| > |y|$, the maximum must be $|x + y|$, giving $|x| \le |x + y|$. For several terms, put $y = x_2 + \cdots + x_n$, which has $|y| \le \max_{i \ge 2}|x_i| < |x_1|$, and apply the two-term case.

In words: in an ultrametric space every triangle is isosceles, with the two longest sides equal.

blocks.title: The p-adic numbers
blocks.body:
$\mathbb{Q}_p$ is the completion of $\mathbb{Q}$ with respect to $|\cdot|_p$: its elements are equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences of rationals, two sequences being equivalent when their difference tends to 0. Addition and multiplication are done term by term, and $|x|_p = \lim |x_n|_p$. This limit exists and is eventually constant when $x \neq 0$ (by the strict triangle inequality, $|x_n|_p = |x_m|_p$ once $|x_n - x_m|_p < |x_m|_p$), so $|\cdot|_p$ takes the same values $p^n$, $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, on $\mathbb{Q}_p^\times$ as on $\mathbb{Q}^\times$, and $v_p$ extends to $\mathbb{Q}_p^\times$.

The $p$-adic integers are $\mathbb{Z}_p = \{x \in \mathbb{Q}_p : |x|_p \le 1\}$. By the ultrametric inequality this set is closed under addition and multiplication, so it is a subring.

blocks.title: Convergence of series
blocks.body: In $\mathbb{Q}_p$ a series $\sum a_n$ converges if and only if $a_n \to 0$.

If the series converges, $a_n = S_n - S_{n-1} \to 0$, as in any normed field. Conversely, for $m > n$,
$$|S_m - S_n|_p = |a_{n+1} + \cdots + a_m|_p \le \max_{n < k \le m} |a_k|_p,$$
which is small when $n$ is large. So the partial sums form a Cauchy sequence, which converges because $\mathbb{Q}_p$ is complete. This is far simpler than real analysis, where $\sum \frac1n$ diverges although $\frac1n \to 0$.

blocks.title: Digit expansions and structure
blocks.body:
1. Every $x \in \mathbb{Z}_p$ can be written uniquely as $x = \sum_{i \ge 0} a_i p^i$ with $a_i \in \{0, 1, \dots, p - 1\}$, and every such series converges to an element of $\mathbb{Z}_p$. The integer $r_n = \sum_{i < n} a_i p^i$ is the unique integer in $[0, p^n)$ with $|x - r_n|_p \le p^{-n}$, and $x \mapsto r_n$ gives a ring isomorphism $\mathbb{Z}_p/p^n\mathbb{Z}_p \cong \mathbb{Z}/p^n\mathbb{Z}$.
2. The units of $\mathbb{Z}_p$ are $\mathbb{Z}_p^\times = \{x : |x|_p = 1\}$, the elements with $a_0 \ne 0$. Every nonzero $x \in \mathbb{Q}_p$ is uniquely $x = p^n u$ with $n = v_p(x) \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $u \in \mathbb{Z}_p^\times$; so $\mathbb{Q}_p$ consists of the expansions $\sum_{i \ge n} a_i p^i$ with finitely many negative powers.
3. $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is compact.

blocks.title: Proof (main points)
blocks.body:
1. Fix $n$. Since $\mathbb{Q}$ is dense in $\mathbb{Q}_p$, pick a rational $y$ with $|x - y|_p \le p^{-n}$; then $|y|_p \le 1$, so $y = \frac{a}{b}$ with $p \nmid b$. Let $r \in [0, p^n)$ be the integer with $r \equiv a b^{-1} \pmod{p^n}$. Then $y - r = \frac{a - br}{b}$ has numerator divisible by $p^n$, so $|y - r|_p \le p^{-n}$ and hence $|x - r|_p \le p^{-n}$. If $r, r'$ both work, then $|r - r'|_p \le p^{-n}$, so $p^n \mid r - r'$, and as $|r - r'| < p^n$ we get $r = r'$. Uniqueness forces $r_{n+1} \equiv r_n \pmod{p^n}$, that is $r_{n+1} = r_n + a_n p^n$ with a digit $a_n$, and $r_n \to x$. Conversely, a digit series converges by the previous theorem, and its limit has $|\cdot|_p \le 1$. The map $x \mapsto r_n$ respects sums and products modulo $p^n$ and has kernel $\{|x|_p \le p^{-n}\} = p^n\mathbb{Z}_p$.

2. If $|x|_p = 1$ then $|x^{-1}|_p = 1$, so $x^{-1} \in \mathbb{Z}_p$; if $|x|_p < 1$ then $|x^{-1}|_p > 1$, so $x$ is not a unit. For $x \ne 0$ with $v_p(x) = n$, the element $u = p^{-n}x$ has $|u|_p = 1$.

3. $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is closed in the complete space $\mathbb{Q}_p$, so complete, and for each $n$ it is covered by the $p^n$ balls of radius $p^{-n}$ around $0, 1, \dots, p^n - 1$, so totally bounded. A complete totally bounded metric space is compact (see [[compactness]]).

blocks.title: Solving equations: Hensel, squares, local and global
blocks.body:
Hensel's lemma becomes a statement about roots in $\mathbb{Z}_p$: if $f$ is a polynomial with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}_p$ and $a \in \mathbb{Z}$ satisfies $f(a) \equiv 0 \pmod p$ and $f'(a) \not\equiv 0 \pmod p$, then $f$ has exactly one root $\alpha \in \mathbb{Z}_p$ with $\alpha \equiv a \pmod p$. Indeed the lemma produces roots $r_n$ modulo $p^n$, each lifting the last; they form a Cauchy sequence whose limit $\alpha$ satisfies $f(\alpha) = 0$ by continuity of polynomials.

For example, which elements of $\mathbb{Q}_p$ are squares, for odd $p$? Write $x = p^n u$. If $x = y^2$ then $n = 2v_p(y)$ is even and $u = (p^{-n/2}y)^2$, so $u \bmod p$ is a [[quadratic-residues|quadratic residue]]. Conversely, if $n$ is even and $u \equiv a^2 \pmod p$ with $p \nmid a$, apply Hensel to $X^2 - u$: its derivative $2a$ is nonzero modulo $p$ because $p$ is odd. So $x$ is a square exactly when $v_p(x)$ is even and $u \bmod p$ is a nonzero square. (For $p = 2$ the rule is that a unit $u$ is a square in $\mathbb{Z}_2$ exactly when $u \equiv 1 \pmod 8$. Odd squares are $\equiv 1 \pmod 8$. Conversely, let $k \ge 3$. If $y, y'$ are odd and $y'^2 \equiv y^2 \pmod{2^k}$, then $2^k$ divides $(y' - y)(y' + y)$; both factors are even and their sum $2y'$ is $\equiv 2 \pmod 4$, so one factor is $\equiv 2 \pmod 4$ and the other is divisible by $2^{k-1}$. Hence $y' \equiv \pm y \pmod{2^{k-1}}$, so each odd square modulo $2^k$ comes from exactly four residues, and the $2^{k-1}$ odd residues give $2^{k-3}$ different squares. All of them are $\equiv 1 \pmod 8$, and there are exactly $2^{k-3}$ residues $\equiv 1 \pmod 8$, so each $u \equiv 1 \pmod 8$ is a square modulo every $2^k$. Choosing $y_k$ with $y_k^2 \equiv u \pmod{2^k}$, compactness of $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gives a convergent subsequence, whose limit $y$ has $y^2 = u$.)

This gives quick proofs of insolubility. The equation $x^2 = 2$ has no solution in $\mathbb{Q}_3$, since 2 is not a square modulo 3, so it certainly has none in $\mathbb{Q}$. It does have one in $\mathbb{Q}_7$, since $2 \equiv 3^2 \pmod 7$, and in $\mathbb{R}$.

The Hasse–Minkowski theorem (stated, not proved here) says that for [[quadratic-forms]] this local information is complete: a quadratic form with rational coefficients has a nontrivial rational zero if and only if it has one in $\mathbb{R}$ and in every $\mathbb{Q}_p$. For cubics this local-to-global principle fails: Selmer showed that $3x^3 + 4y^3 + 5z^3 = 0$ has nontrivial solutions in $\mathbb{R}$ and in every $\mathbb{Q}_p$, but none in $\mathbb{Q}$.

blocks.title: All absolute values of the rationals
blocks.body:
Up to equivalence (replacing $|\cdot|$ by a power $|\cdot|^c$ with $c > 0$), Ostrowski's theorem says that every nontrivial absolute value on $\mathbb{Q}$ is either the usual one, $|\cdot|_\infty$, or $|\cdot|_p$ for exactly one prime $p$. So $\mathbb{R}$ and the fields $\mathbb{Q}_p$ are the only completions of $\mathbb{Q}$, and number theorists treat them on an equal footing, calling them the places of $\mathbb{Q}$.

They are tied together by the product formula: for every nonzero rational $x$,
$$|x|_\infty \prod_p |x|_p = 1.$$
To see this, write $x = \pm\prod_p p^{e_p}$. Then $|x|_\infty = \prod_p p^{e_p}$ and $|x|_p = p^{-e_p}$, and only finitely many factors differ from 1. For example, for $x = \frac{12}{5}$: $\frac{12}{5}\cdot\frac14\cdot\frac13\cdot 5 = 1$.

Topologically $\mathbb{Q}_p$ is strange: every point of a ball is a centre of it, two balls are either disjoint or one contains the other, and the only connected subsets are single points. The ring $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is homeomorphic to the Cantor set.

blocks.title: Expansions of -1 and 1/3 in the 2-adics
blocks.body: Find the 2-adic digits of $-1$ and of $\frac13$, and check the second by multiplication.
blocks.solution:
For $-1$: the geometric series $\sum_{i \ge 0} 2^i$ converges because $|2^i|_2 \to 0$, and its partial sums $2^n - 1$ satisfy $|(2^n - 1) - (-1)|_2 = 2^{-n} \to 0$. So $-1 = \cdots 1111_2$, all digits 1. (In base $p$, $-1$ has all digits $p - 1$.)

For $\frac13$: we need $r_n \in [0, 2^n)$ with $3 r_n \equiv 1 \pmod{2^n}$. One finds $r_1 = 1$, $r_2 = 3$, $r_3 = 3$, $r_4 = 11$, $r_5 = 11$, $r_6 = 43$: the digits are $a_0 = 1$, $a_1 = 1$, and then $0, 1, 0, 1, \dots$ alternating. Summing, $1 + \sum_{k \ge 0} 2^{2k+1} = 1 + \frac{2}{1 - 4} = 1 - \frac23 = \frac13$, using the geometric series in $\mathbb{Q}_2$.

Check: $3 \cdot \frac13 = \frac13 + 2\cdot\frac13$. Adding $\cdots 0101011$ and $\cdots 1010110$ digit by digit from the right: $1 + 0 = 1$; $1 + 1 = 0$ carry 1; then each column is $0 + 1 + 1$ or $1 + 0 + 1$, giving 0 and carrying 1 for ever. The result is $\cdots 0001 = 1$.

blocks.title: A square root of -1 in the 5-adics
blocks.body: Show that $-1$ is a square in $\mathbb{Q}_5$, and find the first four digits of the square root that is $\equiv 2 \pmod 5$.
blocks.solution:
$2^2 + 1 = 5 \equiv 0 \pmod 5$ and $f'(2) = 4 \not\equiv 0$ for $f(X) = X^2 + 1$, so by Hensel there is a unique $\alpha \in \mathbb{Z}_5$ with $\alpha^2 = -1$ and $\alpha \equiv 2$.

Modulo 25, write $\alpha \equiv 2 + 5t$: then $\alpha^2 + 1 = 5 + 20t + 25t^2 \equiv 5(1 + 4t)$, so $1 + 4t \equiv 0 \pmod 5$, $t = 1$, giving 7. Modulo 125, write $7 + 25t$: $(7 + 25t)^2 + 1 = 50 + 350t + 625t^2 \equiv 25(2 + 14t)$, so $2 + 4t \equiv 0 \pmod 5$, $t = 2$, giving 57. One more step gives 182. So
$$\alpha = 2 + 1\cdot 5 + 2\cdot 5^2 + 1\cdot 5^3 + \cdots,$$
and indeed $182^2 + 1 = 33125 = 5^4 \cdot 53$. The other square root is $-\alpha$, which is $\equiv 3 \pmod 5$.

blocks.title: Harmonic numbers are never integers
blocks.body: Prove that $H_n = 1 + \frac12 + \frac13 + \cdots + \frac1n$ is not an integer for any $n \ge 2$.
blocks.solution:
Let $2^m$ be the largest power of 2 with $2^m \le n$; then $m \ge 1$. Every $k \le n$ other than $2^m$ has $v_2(k) < m$: a $k$ with $v_2(k) \ge m$ is a multiple of $2^m$, and the next multiple $2^{m+1}$ already exceeds $n$. So in the sum $H_n = \sum_{k=1}^n \frac1k$ the term $\frac{1}{2^m}$ has $2$-adic absolute value $2^m$, strictly larger than that of every other term.

By the strict triangle inequality, $|H_n|_2 = 2^m > 1$. But every integer has $|\cdot|_2 \le 1$. So $H_n$ is not an integer. For instance $H_4 = \frac{25}{12}$, and $|\frac{25}{12}|_2 = 4 = 2^2$.

blocks.body:
- Digits run to the left. A $p$-adic integer is like an odometer with infinitely many wheels; carries go on for ever, and that is how $\cdots1111_2 + 1 = 0$.
- $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is not $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, nor the ring $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ of rationals with denominator prime to $p$. That ring is countable and sits densely inside $\mathbb{Z}_p$, which is uncountable.
- $\mathbb{Q}_p$ cannot be made an ordered field. By the square criteria above, $1 - p$ (for odd $p$) and $-7$ (for $p = 2$) are squares in $\mathbb{Q}_p$, yet they are negative rationals, and in an ordered field containing $\mathbb{Q}$ every negative rational is negative and no square is.
- Hensel's lemma needs $f'(a) \not\equiv 0 \pmod p$ in the simple form; for $X^2 - u$ with $p = 2$ that fails, which is why the rule for $p = 2$ is different.

The valuation and congruence tools behind this page are [[p-adic-valuation]], [[lte-zsigmondy]] and [[hensel]]; the completion is the same as for [[real-numbers]]. In algebraic number theory every prime ideal of a ring of integers gives a completion like $\mathbb{Q}_p$ (see [[ideals]]), and the local-to-global philosophy runs from [[quadratic-forms]] to [[elliptic-curves]], where counting points modulo $p$ is the first step towards the conjecture of [[bsd]].

2. Prove that two balls in $\mathbb{Q}_p$ are either disjoint or one contains the other.
3. Show that $\sum_{n \ge 1} n \cdot n! = -1$ in every $\mathbb{Q}_p$. (Hint: compute the partial sums.)
4. For which primes $p$ is $x^2 = 3$ solvable in $\mathbb{Q}_p$? Answer for $p \le 13$, treating $p = 2$ and $p = 3$ separately.

def v(x, p):
    x = F(x); n, d = x.numerator, x.denominator; k = 0
